units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay. Michigan Avenue, over the bridge, and there's a Gothic castle.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: That's Tribune Tower. Finished in 1925.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's thirty-six floors and four hundred and sixty-three feet tall, and it began with a contest.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Of course it did.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1922 the Chicago Tribune turned seventy-five and announced an international competition to design what it called the most beautiful office building in the world.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Modest.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The prize was a hundred thousand dollars, with fifty thousand to the winner.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: More than two hundred and sixty entries arrived from twenty-three countries.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Who won?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A pair of New York architects, Raymond Hood and John Mead Howells.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The style is Gothic Revival. The crown is based on a tower from Rouen Cathedral in France, a thirteenth-century tower, and the lower floors use Art Deco-style piers.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So a medieval church on top of an office block.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Basically. Now come down to the sidewalk, because this is the part you came for.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Look at the base of the walls.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Some stones are different from the rest.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Oh, I see them. There's a little label.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: More than a hundred and forty of those.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They're fragments from famous places around the world, set into the walls.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Which ones?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A piece of the Great Wall of China.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A piece of the Parthenon in Athens.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A piece from the Taj Mahal. A piece of the Great Pyramid at Giza.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A fragment of Notre-Dame, one from the Alamo, one from the Colosseum.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the Berlin Wall.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: That too. Walk along and find it.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The labels say where each piece came from.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Who collected them?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Colonel Robert McCormick, the Tribune's co-publisher, spent decades collecting.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Tribune correspondents brought back the earliest pieces at his request, and readers contributed specimens too.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So the newspaper's reporters were also carrying rocks.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In their luggage. Yes.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: One more. There's a moon rock in there?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: There's a commemorative stone for the Apollo missions.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And one guide says it's actually ordinary earth stone, honoring the moon missions, not a real lunar rock.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: A pretend moon rock. A decoy.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A tribute. It's fine.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay, that's kind of delightful.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Take your time, and pause here.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: You can circle the building. When you're ready, the second stop is about eighteen minutes' walk northwest, through the River North gallery district.
